title: HIV Prevention: Test, PrEP, PEP, and Link to Care
system: Infectious Disease / Sexual Health / Public Health
bottomLine: HIV prevention is proactive: offer appropriate testing, PrEP to people with ongoing substantial exposure risk, and time-sensitive PEP after a significant recent exposure. A reactive screening test requires confirmatory testing and linkage to HIV care rather than disclosure as a final diagnosis.
recognize: Risk assessment includes sexual exposure, injection equipment sharing, partner HIV status and viral suppression, recent STIs and patient preference for prevention.
differentiate: PrEP is taken before or during ongoing risk; PEP is started after a discrete exposure and is time-sensitive; U=U means a person with sustained undetectable HIV viral load does not sexually transmit HIV.
assessment: Use nonjudgmental sexual and substance-use history, exposure timing and type, pregnancy possibility, renal function and hepatitis B status when relevant to antiretroviral selection.
workup: Use current HIV antigen/antibody and supplemental testing algorithms; baseline and follow-up testing for PrEP/PEP follows contemporary Canadian guidance and local program protocols.
management: Start PEP urgently when indicated rather than waiting for every source-person result; offer PrEP for ongoing risk and link newly diagnosed patients rapidly to antiretroviral care.
medicationSafety: Tenofovir-containing prevention regimens require renal and hepatitis B context; stopping some tenofovir-based regimens in chronic hepatitis B requires appropriate follow-up.
redFlags: High-risk exposure within the PEP window
Acute HIV syndrome after recent exposure
counselling: Explain U=U accurately, condom and STI prevention choices, adherence and the distinction between a preliminary reactive screen and confirmed diagnosis.
followUp: Complete scheduled HIV testing after PEP and ongoing monitoring during PrEP according to the current Canadian pathway.
examTrap: Waiting several days for the source person's final HIV testing before starting indicated PEP.
oneLinePearl: PEP is a clock; PrEP is a prevention plan.
sourceBasis: PHAC STBBI Prevention Guide: Biomedical Prevention 2025-2026

title: Syphilis: Stage the Infection Before You Choose the Follow-Up
bottomLine: Syphilis is staged from history, examination and serology because stage affects treatment and follow-up. Pregnancy, neurologic or ocular disease and possible congenital infection require urgent specialist or public-health coordination.
recognize: Primary syphilis can cause a painless chancre; secondary disease can cause diffuse rash including palms/soles, lymphadenopathy and systemic features; latent disease has positive serology without symptoms.
differentiate: A positive treponemal test can remain positive after prior treatment; nontreponemal titre and history help assess activity and treatment response.
assessment: Assess prior syphilis testing/treatment, pregnancy, neurologic/ocular/otic symptoms, sexual partners and HIV risk.
workup: Interpret treponemal and nontreponemal tests together and compare prior titres; evaluate suspected neurosyphilis, ocular or otic disease urgently with experienced consultation.
management: Use current PHAC stage-specific penicillin-based treatment; benzathine penicillin remains essential in pregnancy, and public-health partner notification is required according to jurisdiction.
medicationSafety: A Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction can occur after treatment; it is not a penicillin allergy and is especially relevant in pregnancy.
counselling: Explain follow-up titres and partner management without stigma.
followUp: Repeat nontreponemal titres at guideline-recommended intervals and assess for reinfection or inadequate response.
examTrap: Calling a persistently positive treponemal test treatment failure after adequately treated past syphilis.
oneLinePearl: Treponemal tests remember; nontreponemal titres help track activity.

title: Gonorrhea and Chlamydia: Site-Specific Testing, Current Treatment, Test-of-Cure Rules
bottomLine: STI testing must match exposed anatomic sites. Canadian gonorrhea guidance changed again in June 2026, so use the current PHAC regimen and current culture/test-of-cure recommendations rather than memorized older doses.
recognize: Urethral or cervical infection may be symptomatic or asymptomatic; pharyngeal and rectal infections are commonly missed if testing follows anatomy assumptions rather than exposure history.
differentiate: PID, epididymitis, disseminated gonococcal infection and pregnancy require complication-specific management.
assessment: Ask sexual practices and sites of exposure, symptoms, pregnancy, allergies, prior STI, antimicrobial exposure and partner status using inclusive language.
workup: Use NAAT at all exposed sites; obtain gonococcal culture when current PHAC indications apply, including circumstances where susceptibility or treatment-failure assessment matters.
management: Use the current June 2026 PHAC preferred treatment for uncomplicated gonorrhea and treat chlamydia when present or not excluded according to current guidance; manage partners and public-health reporting requirements.
medicationSafety: Avoid obsolete gonorrhea regimens because resistance and national recommendations have changed; pregnancy changes chlamydia treatment choices.
counselling: Discuss abstinence or barrier use until treatment and partner-management requirements are satisfied and offer HIV prevention where relevant.
followUp: Follow current PHAC test-of-cure and retesting recommendations, particularly for gonorrhea where 2026 guidance expanded culture and test-of-cure considerations.
examTrap: Testing only urine after a patient reports receptive oral and anal sex.
oneLinePearl: Test the sites that were exposed, not the sites you assume were exposed.

title: Genital Herpes and HPV: Diagnose, Counsel, Prevent
bottomLine: Genital herpes is best confirmed from active lesions with type-specific molecular testing when available; HPV commonly clears spontaneously, while persistent oncogenic HPV drives cervical and other cancers. Management includes symptom control, transmission counselling and vaccination where eligible.
recognize: HSV can cause painful grouped vesicles/ulcers and may be atypical; genital warts are usually caused by low-oncogenic-risk HPV types.
differentiate: Syphilitic chancres are often painless; aphthous, traumatic and inflammatory ulcers can mimic HSV.
assessment: Assess lesion timing, recurrence, pregnancy, immune status, cervical screening status and partner concerns.
workup: Swab active HSV lesions for NAAT when possible; routine HPV testing is performed through cervical-screening pathways rather than as a general STI panel.
management: Use episodic or suppressive antiviral therapy for HSV based on severity and recurrence/transmission goals; treat visible warts selectively and maintain appropriate HPV vaccination/screening.
medicationSafety: Do not use topical podophyllin-type wart products in pregnancy unless specifically supported; pregnancy near delivery with HSV requires obstetric planning.
counselling: Explain asymptomatic HSV shedding, condom limitations and that HPV infection is common and does not prove recent infidelity.
followUp: Coordinate obstetric care for HSV in pregnancy and maintain cervical screening according to the current provincial pathway.
examTrap: Ordering a blood HPV test or treating an HPV-positive cervical screening result as proof of visible genital warts.
oneLinePearl: HSV is a lesion-and-shedding disease; HPV is a persistence-and-screening disease.

title: Lyme Disease: Exposure, Stage, and Objective Findings
bottomLine: Early localized Lyme disease with a classic expanding erythema migrans lesion after plausible tick exposure is a clinical diagnosis and should be treated without waiting for serology. Later neurologic, cardiac or arthritic disease uses stage-appropriate testing and treatment.
recognize: Erythema migrans expands over days and may not look like a perfect bull's-eye; facial palsy, meningitis, carditis and large-joint arthritis are later manifestations.
differentiate: Local tick-bite hypersensitivity is usually small and early; cellulitis and tinea can mimic rash; nonspecific fatigue alone is not diagnostic.
assessment: Assess geography/travel, tick exposure duration if known, rash timing, neurologic/cardiac/joint symptoms and pregnancy.
workup: Do not order serology for a classic early erythema migrans lesion because antibodies may not yet be detectable; use two-tier serology for appropriate later manifestations.
management: Use stage- and age-appropriate antibiotic treatment according to current Canadian guidance; urgently evaluate syncope, AV block or severe neurologic disease.
medicationSafety: Antibiotic choice varies by age, pregnancy and manifestation; prolonged unproven antibiotic courses for nonspecific post-treatment symptoms can cause harm.
counselling: Teach tick checks, prompt removal and current prevention strategies without falsely implying every tick bite causes Lyme disease.
followUp: Persistent objective symptoms require reassessment; serology should not be used to prove cure.
examTrap: Waiting for a positive Lyme serology before treating a classic erythema migrans lesion.
oneLinePearl: Classic erythema migrans is treated clinically because early serology can be negative.

title: Fever in a Returned Traveller: Malaria Until Excluded When Exposure Fits
bottomLine: A febrile traveller returning from a malaria-risk region requires urgent malaria testing even if prophylaxis was taken. Travel geography and incubation period rapidly narrow the differential for malaria, dengue, enteric fever and other imported infections.
recognize: Malaria can present nonspecifically with fever, chills, headache, GI symptoms or altered mental status and can deteriorate rapidly.
differentiate: Dengue often produces cytopenias and myalgias and carries bleeding/plasma-leak risk; enteric fever and viral illnesses can overlap.
assessment: Ask exact countries/regions, dates, rural/urban exposure, mosquito/tick/freshwater/animal/food contacts, prophylaxis/vaccines and pregnancy.
workup: Obtain urgent malaria testing with repeat testing if clinical suspicion remains and initial testing is negative; use CBC, liver/renal testing and targeted cultures or molecular tests based on travel pattern.
management: Treat severe malaria immediately through hospital/infectious-disease pathways; use cause-specific therapy and public-health notification when required.
medicationSafety: Avoid NSAIDs in suspected dengue because of bleeding risk; pregnancy changes antimalarial treatment choices.
counselling: Teach that malaria can occur despite prophylaxis and may present months after travel depending on species.
followUp: Ensure all pending travel-infection tests and public-health actions are closed-loop.
examTrap: Diagnosing influenza in a febrile returned traveller from a malaria area without asking travel details or ordering malaria testing.
oneLinePearl: Fever plus malaria geography is malaria until appropriately excluded.

title: Occupational Blood Exposure: Wash, Risk-Stratify, Act Fast
bottomLine: After needlestick or mucosal blood exposure, perform immediate local first aid, document the exposure, assess source and exposure risk, verify hepatitis B immunity and start indicated HIV PEP as soon as possible rather than waiting for every baseline result.
recognize: Percutaneous injury with a hollow-bore needle and visible blood generally carries more risk than intact-skin contact.
differentiate: HIV, HBV and HCV have different prevention pathways; there is no HCV PEP, so follow-up testing matters.
assessment: Clarify device, depth, fluid, source status/risk, worker vaccination/anti-HBs history, pregnancy and timing.
workup: Obtain baseline source and exposed-person testing with consent according to local occupational-health/public-health law and protocol.
management: Initiate HIV PEP urgently when indicated, provide HBV vaccine or immunoglobulin according to immunity and exposure status, and arrange HCV follow-up testing.
medicationSafety: Do not delay indicated PEP solely because source testing is pending; check renal function and interactions for the selected regimen.
redFlags: High-risk exposure within the PEP window
counselling: Explain actual transmission risk and reduce shame/anxiety while emphasizing follow-up.
followUp: Ensure serial HIV/HCV testing and occupational-health documentation are completed.
examTrap: Waiting for the source patient's final HIV result before offering time-sensitive PEP after a high-risk exposure.
oneLinePearl: Blood-exposure care has a clock: clean, assess, prevent, follow.

title: Immunization Catch-Up: Do Not Restart a Vaccine Series Because It Was Delayed
bottomLine: Interrupted vaccine series are generally continued, not restarted. Use age, prior documented doses, risk factors, immune status, pregnancy and current NACI guidance to build a catch-up plan while respecting provincial or territorial funded schedules.
recognize: Missing records are common in newcomers, people without primary care and adults whose childhood schedules differed.
differentiate: A national recommendation and a publicly funded provincial program are not always identical.
assessment: Review reliable records, age, pregnancy, immune status, splenic function, chronic disease, travel/occupation and prior vaccine reactions.
workup: Serology is useful only for selected vaccine-preventable diseases and circumstances; do not order broad immunity panels routinely when revaccination is safe and appropriate.
management: Build a catch-up schedule using current Canadian Immunization Guide minimum intervals and age/risk recommendations; co-administer compatible vaccines when appropriate.
medicationSafety: Live vaccines are generally contraindicated in pregnancy and significant immunosuppression; timing with immunoglobulin/blood products can affect live-vaccine effectiveness.
redFlags: Suspected anaphylaxis to a prior dose/component
counselling: Explain that extra doses of many vaccines are preferable to leaving a susceptible patient unprotected when records cannot be recovered, when permitted by current guidance.
followUp: Document doses and next due dates in the provincial/territorial record when available.
examTrap: Restarting a hepatitis B or other multidose series because years passed after the first dose.
oneLinePearl: Delayed vaccine series continue; they usually do not restart.

title: Vaccination in Immunocompromise: Inactivated Often Safe, Live Often Not
bottomLine: Immunocompromised patients often need more—not fewer—vaccines, but product type, timing and expected response differ. Live vaccines may be contraindicated during significant immunosuppression, while inactivated vaccines can often be given safely though response may be reduced.
recognize: Immunosuppression includes specific biologic or cytotoxic therapy, transplant, some primary immunodeficiencies and high-dose systemic corticosteroid exposure.
differentiate: Being immunocompromised is not a blanket contraindication to all vaccines.
assessment: Identify diagnosis, medication type and timing, transplant status, vaccine history, household contacts and future immunosuppression plans.
workup: Serologic response testing is reserved for selected situations such as hepatitis B or specific immune disorders.
management: Use current Canadian Immunization Guide and therapy-specific timing; vaccinate before immunosuppression when feasible and use additional indicated pneumococcal, zoster, RSV, influenza or other vaccines according to current NACI guidance.
medicationSafety: Live vaccine exposure during significant immunosuppression can cause disease; vaccine timing around B-cell depletion and other therapies materially affects response.
redFlags: Live vaccine planned during contraindicating immunosuppression
counselling: Explain that reduced immune response does not mean vaccination is useless and that household immunization can add protection.
followUp: Reassess vaccine needs as therapy changes.
examTrap: Withholding influenza and other inactivated vaccines simply because a patient is immunocompromised.
oneLinePearl: Immunocompromise changes vaccine strategy; it does not erase vaccination.
sourceBasis: Canadian Immunization Guide: Immunization of Immunocompromised Persons updated 2026

title: Penicillin Allergy and Stewardship: Verify the Label Before Broadening Therapy
bottomLine: Many penicillin-allergy labels are inaccurate and push patients toward broader, less effective or more toxic antibiotics. Clarify the original reaction, timing and severity, and use delabelling or supervised challenge pathways for low-risk histories when appropriate.
recognize: Isolated remote nausea, headache or family history is not IgE-mediated penicillin allergy; anaphylaxis, SJS/TEN and severe organ reactions are high-risk histories.
differentiate: Immediate urticaria/angioedema differs from delayed benign rash and from severe cutaneous adverse reaction.
assessment: Ask exact drug, age/time of reaction, latency after dose, symptoms, treatment/hospitalization and subsequent beta-lactam tolerance.
workup: Use direct oral challenge or allergy testing according to validated low- versus high-risk pathways; do not challenge patients with severe cutaneous or organ reactions.
management: Remove inaccurate allergy labels after successful validated assessment and choose the narrowest effective antibiotic for the infection.
medicationSafety: Do not perform unsupervised drug challenge after anaphylaxis or SJS/TEN history.
counselling: Explain why an accurate allergy record improves future infection treatment.
followUp: Update all accessible medication records after delabelling.
examTrap: Automatically prescribing a fluoroquinolone because the chart says 'penicillin allergy—upset stomach'.
oneLinePearl: An allergy label is a clinical history, not a permanent fact.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada antimicrobial stewardship recommendations

title: Antimicrobial Stewardship: Treat Infection, Not Colonization
bottomLine: Antibiotics should have a bacterial syndrome, likely pathogen, appropriate drug, dose, route and duration. Positive cultures do not always equal infection, and every empiric regimen should have a reassessment or stop point.
recognize: Asymptomatic bacteriuria, airway colonization and positive superficial wound cultures commonly lead to unnecessary antibiotics.
differentiate: Colonization means organism present without clinical infection; contamination means the specimen itself is unreliable.
assessment: Define the infection syndrome and severity before reading culture results in isolation.
workup: Obtain cultures before antibiotics when results will alter therapy and delay is safe; avoid cultures when a positive result is likely to drive treatment of colonization.
management: Start empiric antibiotics when bacterial infection is likely and delay would harm, then narrow, stop or convert IV to oral when clinical and microbiologic data support it.
medicationSafety: Antibiotics can cause C. difficile, renal/hepatic injury, QT effects, drug interactions and resistance selection.
redFlags: Persistent fever despite appropriate source control
counselling: Explain why not prescribing an antibiotic can be an active safety decision rather than withholding care.
followUp: Set a culture-result and antibiotic-duration review date at initiation.
examTrap: Treating a positive urine culture in an asymptomatic nonpregnant older adult because the organism has a high colony count.
oneLinePearl: Culture results answer 'what grew'; the patient answers 'is there infection?'.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Using Antibiotics Wisely

title: Reportable Disease and Outbreak Care: Treat the Patient, Protect the Population
bottomLine: Some infections require public-health notification, isolation, contact management or outbreak action in addition to individual treatment. Exact reportable-disease lists and timelines are provincial or territorial, so verify local law rather than assuming one Canada-wide operational rule.
recognize: Measles, invasive meningococcal disease, TB, many STBBIs and foodborne/outbreak-associated infections can trigger public-health action.
differentiate: Clinical suspicion may be sufficient to start isolation or notify public health before laboratory confirmation for some high-consequence infections.
assessment: Ask exposure setting, travel, occupation, congregate living, school/daycare, vulnerable contacts and onset dates.
workup: Collect public-health-relevant specimens correctly and coordinate specialized testing when required.
management: Use appropriate isolation, treatment or post-exposure prophylaxis and promptly notify the jurisdictional public-health authority when legal criteria are met.
medicationSafety: Post-exposure prophylaxis and vaccine decisions are disease-specific and time-sensitive.
redFlags: Suspected measles in a health-care setting
counselling: Explain confidentiality boundaries and why contact follow-up may be required.
followUp: Document notification and responsibility for contact/outbreak actions.
examTrap: Waiting for final lab confirmation before taking any infection-control action in a highly suspected measles case.
oneLinePearl: Public-health infections have two patients: the person in front of you and the exposed community.
